nameStory: The pinfish gets its memorable name from the sharp, needle-like spines on its dorsal fin that can deliver a surprising prick to unwary anglers. These defensive spines are so prominent that they inspired not just the common name 'pinfish,' but also the alternative name 'pin perch.' It's a fish that literally announces itself through touch!
description: The pinfish is a small, disc-shaped saltwater fish that belongs to the porgy and seabream family. These silvery fish typically grow to about 4-8 inches long and have a distinctly compressed, oval body profile. They're characterized by their sharp dorsal spines, small mouth, and subtle vertical bars along their sides. While primarily southern fish, pinfish occasionally venture into New England's warmer coastal waters during summer months.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Sharp, prominent spines along the dorsal fin that feel like needles when touched - handle with care! The spiny portion of the dorsal fin is particularly noticeable.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly compressed, oval body that feels firm and muscular, much deeper than it is wide, giving it an almost diamond-like profile when viewed from the side.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Silvery overall with 4-6 faint vertical bars along the sides that may be barely visible in bright light but become more apparent in shade or when the fish is stressed.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth with small, incisor-like teeth that feel rough if you run your finger along them - adapted for scraping algae and small prey.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Generally small fish, typically 4-8 inches long, feeling surprisingly solid and hefty for their size due to their deep, compressed body.

habitat: In New England, pinfish are rare visitors found only in the warmest shallow coastal waters during peak summer, particularly around eelgrass beds, sandy bottoms near jetties, and protected bays. They prefer areas with some vegetation or structure where they can find algae and small invertebrates to feed on. Look for them in water depths of 3-15 feet in places like Cape Cod's warmer south-facing shores.

seasonality.spring: Absent from New England waters - still in southern wintering areas. Any spring sightings would be exceptionally rare stragglers.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for rare New England sightings, particularly in July and August when water temperatures reach their warmest. Most likely to be found during heat waves in shallow, protected waters.
seasonality.fall: Early fall may still produce occasional sightings in very warm years, but fish begin moving south as temperatures drop. Late fall sightings would be very unusual.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England waters - these fish cannot tolerate cold temperatures and migrate south to survive winter.

funFact: Pinfish are like underwater landscapers - they play a crucial role in maintaining healthy seagrass beds by constantly 'mowing' algae that would otherwise smother the grass, but they occasionally get so enthusiastic that they can actually overgraze and damage the very habitats they help maintain!
confusionNotes: Pinfish might be confused with young scup (porgy) since both are silver, disc-shaped members of the same family. However, scup lack the pinfish's prominent dorsal spines and distinct vertical bars - remember 'pins have spines' to distinguish the pinfish's needle-sharp dorsal fin.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be confused by the alternative names 'pin perch' and 'sand perch' - pinfish aren't actually perches at all, but members of the porgy family. This naming confusion arose because early settlers often called any small, spiny fish a 'perch' regardless of its true family relationships.
compareHints: Pinfish are the only species in their genus Lagodon, making them unique among New England porgies. Compared to their closest relatives like scup and sheepshead in the same family, pinfish are smaller, have more prominent dorsal spines, and display clearer vertical barring on their sides. Unlike the larger, more robust scup, pinfish maintain their compressed, delicate appearance throughout their lives.
